result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_all_simple_paths()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find all simple paths between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L18536-L18680){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_all_simple_paths( source, target, cutoff=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![All simple paths](/assets/graphs/algo-all-simple-paths.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A graph with source s and target t on the sides, showing three distinct simple paths between them: a two-hop path through the top in accent, a two-hop path straight through the middle in a lighter accent tint, and a three-hop path along the bottom in teal, each rendered in its own distinct style." width="100%"} A simple path is a path with no repeated nodes. This method uses depth-first search with backtracking to enumerate all possible simple paths from source to target. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node (integer ID or string label). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Target node (integer ID or string label). [cutoff]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum path length (number of edges) to consider. If `None`, no limit is applied. Useful for preventing excessive computation in large graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list of lists of str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of paths, where each path is a list of node labels from source to target. Returns an empty list if no paths exist. ::: ## Algorithm {.doc-algorithm} - uses DFS with backtracking - time complexity: O(n!) worst case (exponential in path length) - space complexity: O(n) for recursion stack - best for: Finding alternative routes, analyzing network redundancy, path enumeration ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - **Network Redundancy**: Find backup routes in communication networks - **Social Network Analysis**: Discover indirect connections between people - **Logistics**: Identify alternative delivery routes - **Knowledge Graphs**: Trace reasoning paths between concepts - **Biology**: Analyze metabolic pathways with multiple routes ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The number of simple paths between two nodes can blow up exponentially: the complete graph $K_n$ has $(n - 2)!$ simple paths between any two vertices, and even moderately dense random graphs quickly exceed practical enumeration. The `cutoff=` parameter is the standard escape hatch, capping the search at a fixed number of edges, and it should almost always be supplied on graphs beyond a few dozen nodes. Because every path is materialized in memory, the aggregate size of the result is what constrains large runs more than sheer traversal cost. If ranked *shortest* paths are the goal rather than every simple path, `k_shortest_paths()` uses Yen's algorithm to surface just the top $k$ efficiently. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A diamond-shaped graph has two distinct routes from `A` to `D`, so both are returned: ::: {#a02d5d74 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("A", "C") .add_edge("B", "D") .add_edge("C", "D") ) paths = graph.get_all_simple_paths("A", "D") # Returns [['A', 'B', 'D'], ['A', 'C', 'D']] paths ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'B', 'D'], ['A', 'C', 'D']] ``` ::: ::: Adding a `cutoff` limits how many edges a path may use, useful for pruning long detours in larger graphs: ::: {#f1fbb7b2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_node(label="E") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "D") .add_edge("D", "E") .add_edge("A", "E") ) # Only the direct A->E edge satisfies a 2-edge cutoff short_paths = graph.get_all_simple_paths("A", "E", cutoff=2) # Returns 1 len(short_paths) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cfb58447 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Without a cutoff, the longer A->B->C->D->E route is included too all_paths = graph.get_all_simple_paths("A", "E") # Returns 2 len(all_paths) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: This also makes it easy to check how many redundant routes exist between two points in a network: ::: {#78710c28 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} network = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="Server1") .add_node(label="Router1") .add_node(label="Router2") .add_node(label="Server2") .add_edge("Server1", "Router1") .add_edge("Server1", "Router2") .add_edge("Router1", "Server2") .add_edge("Router2", "Server2") ) routes = network.get_all_simple_paths("Server1", "Server2") # Returns 2 (backup routes via Router1 and Router2) len(routes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 2 ``` ::: :::
